title: Chapter 151 – The Message
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

They let him sleep for three days, and for two of them he is not sure which of them is sleeping.

It is a pleasant confusion. He wakes in the narrow bed in the old house, in the room that was his as a boy, under a quilt that smells of wood-smoke and Qinghe's soap, and lies for a long time looking at the beams. The light is gray and clean. Rain ticks on the tiles. Somewhere in the house a kettle is whistling, a door is banging, a child is asking a question in a high carrying voice. And behind his eyes, in a small round room with a stove, someone is turning the pages of a book.

Good morning, says the boy.

Good morning.

You snore.

I am told. He smiles at the ceiling. Do you want the window?

Could I?

Of course.

It is the easiest thing in the world. He lets go, the way he let go on the night of the Core, and the old body, which is his and not his, sits up in bed and stretches, and a small clear voice says "Oh!" in sheer delight. His own hands, white-haired, veined, come up in front of his face, and the boy turns them over, one and then the other, slowly, with wonder.

They're big, says the boy.

They are old.

They're good. A pause. Can I touch the quilt?

He does. He spends nearly an hour in the room, touching things: the quilt, the wall, the cold iron of the window-latch, a bowl of persimmons that Qinghe has left on the sill. He smells them. He bites one and the juice runs down his chin, and he laughs, aloud, a high rusty amazed laugh, and the door opens and Qinghe stands there with a tray, in her blue smock, with her hand pressed to her mouth.

"It's good," says the boy, with his mouth full. "Mama, it's so good."

She sets the tray down very carefully. She sits on the edge of the bed. She does not say anything. She takes a corner of her apron and wipes the juice from his chin, and her hand does not shake.

* * *

On the fourth day, they go to get the stone.

The family comes, because the family comes. It is a small procession down the seven hundred and one steps in the early morning: Qinghe with her lantern, Yue with Pebble on her shoulder, Tian Mo a pace behind, Feng on a litter carried by two nephews. Bell has insisted on coming and has been told to stay at the clinic and has refused. Zhao and her husband follow, with the baby. Nobody speaks. The stair is cold. The lamps in the niches burn blue.

The Dock is the same. The wall of the Gate stands at the far end of the round room, black and smooth, closed like an eye. The cot is still by the south wall. The flat stone in front of the wall bears the faint round mark where a man has sat cross-legged every night for fourteen years. And on the shelf beside it, in the shadow, between a chipped teapot and a roll of Sang Ruo's blue cloth, lies a small gray object about the size of a hen's egg.

He has not touched it in fifty years. It was Lan Tong's gift, brought from the Quiet Seat, from Sang Ruo's neck: fragment three, the third stone. It looks like a river pebble. It is dull and smooth and faintly warm, with a groove down one side as if a thumb had worn it. He picks it up. It weighs almost nothing.

That's it? says the boy.

That is it.

It looks like the one in the garden. The one I used to put in my mouth.

I know. He turns it over. I think it was made to look like that on purpose. Something a child might pick up.

Pebble shifts on Yue's shoulder. His voice, deep now, carries across the vast dim room without effort, and it has not lost the strange resonance of that first night. "It is a key. It is not a very good one. The sixth door was made to open from the other side, and this will only knock."

"Knock?"

"Once." The black eyes blink slowly. "The Gate will run both ways, one time, for as long as the stone burns. You will speak. He will hear. He will answer. Then the stone will be ash, and this Dock will go dark."

"Dark?"

"The Gate is the root of it. When the last message is sent, the thing that feeds this Dock will be spent. The wall will be wall. The stair will be a stair. The Interface, which your family calls a gift, will lose its anchor here. It will have to find another."

Jian does not look at the panel. He knows what it will say.

Standby, he thinks. Reduced to a status line. It is the thing he has been afraid of, in the back of his mind, ever since the night at the Dock in the first year of the Sect, when the panel went dark and said Booting. All his advantages. All his clean small numbers. The knife in the sleeve. He would not be, in any ordinary sense, helpless: he has a Golden Core, and the wisdom of eighty-six years, and a family that loves him. But he would be an old man in a quiet room.

It's all right, says the boy.

You don't have to say that.

I know. But it is. A small hand rests, in the room, on his. We never needed it very much. It was just the way you could see.

Jian closes his eyes. He thinks of the first panel, in the Reed Courtyard, on a cold night, seventy years ago, a pale blue screen in a dark head, and a child's voice somewhere in the dark saying oh.

I think, he says carefully, that you were there, for that one.

I was scared.

So was I.

Good, says the boy. Then we match.

* * *

Feng speaks first, from his litter, with his head cocked and his thin hands folded on his chest.

"Before you do it," he says. "I want you to know what I hear."

Everyone turns.

"The wall is not asleep. It hasn't been since the night of the Core." His voice is quiet and slightly dreamy, the voice of a man describing a dream. "It's leaning. The way a man leans toward a door when he's heard a footstep on the other side. There's someone there, Brother. I don't know who. I can't hear a voice. But I can hear him listening."

"The stored copy," says Jian.

"Maybe." Feng frowns. "Or maybe something else. Something that came with him. There's another note under it, very low." He hums it, a deep wavering tone. "I've heard it once before. In the Orchard. In the Mother Tree."

"A tree?"

"A tree," says Yue, signing, and Pebble relays the words with a slight dry edge, "does not hum for six hundred years without a reason."

Qinghe has said nothing. She is sitting on her stool with the basket in her lap, looking at the wall with the flat steady expression she wears when she is doing sums. Now she lifts her head.

"Let me understand this. There is a man, asleep, in another world. He made your Gate. He put a child in your cradle. And he has been asking, through the wall, whether the child is well."

"Yes."

"And you are going to tell him."

"Yes."

"Good." She nods once, briskly, as though a bargain had been struck at a market. "Then I will say what I want to say, and then I will be quiet. If he is the man you say, and he is sorry, I should like him to know that I raised the boy. Both boys. And that he has no cause to be ashamed of the result." Her chin rises. "I would also like him to know that he owes me for fourteen years of suppers."

A faint laugh runs round the ring. It is the first, and it breaks the tension like a hand on a string.

"I'll put it in," says the boy, from the room. His voice is a little shaky. "Is that all right?"

It is more than all right, says Jian. It is the best clause in the letter.

* * *

They do it that afternoon, because there is no reason to wait.

The family stands in a half ring around the flat stone. Jian sits on it, cross-legged, with the third stone in his lap. He has not tied up his hair. It falls white to his shoulders, soft as thistledown, and in the lamp-light he looks, Qinghe thinks, with a sudden pang, like his father.

"Read it," says Yue, signing, and Pebble relays. "The words. Before you say them."

"There are not many."

"Then they will not take long."

He nods. He closes his eyes, and the room dissolves, and he is at the round table with the stove ticking. The boy is already there, in his white shirt, on his chair. There is a sheet of paper on the table and a brush. His small right hand is inky. He has been practicing.

"I wrote it down," says the boy. He pushes the sheet across. "I thought it would be better. If I just said it, I'd forget half."

Jian takes the paper. The characters are round and careful and slightly crooked, the work of a child who has had the best teacher in the world and not quite enough time. He reads.

Dear Mr. Cole.

My name is Lin Jian. I am nine, or I am eighty-six, depending how you count. I am the one who lives in the house.

I am all right. Please do not worry. I have a mother who cooks and a father who falls asleep in the winter and a sister who hears things and a brother who is also me. I have a very big family. There are over a thousand of us now. We grow apples.

I know that you are sorry. I want to say that you do not have to be. I was a baby when you came, and I was lonely, and I did not know I was lonely until he arrived. So I think it worked out. I am not angry. I would like you to know that.

I heard you in the Gate. You asked if I was all right. Nobody has ever asked me that before. Thank you.

There is a tree in the orchard that you gave to somebody a long time ago. It is very big now. I think you should come and see it.

My mother says that you owe her for fourteen years of suppers. She is not joking.

Lin Jian.

He reads it to the end. He sets the paper down. It takes him a minute to find his voice.

"Is there anything you want to change?"

"No."

"You did not mention the others."

"What others?"

"The seven. The ones who came before." Jian looks up. "I do not know what happened to them. I do not know if they are..."

"I don't know either." The boy's voice is small. "I thought we should ask. After. If he answers."

"After."

"Yes." The thin face is very grave. "I think it's polite to say hello first."

Jian laughs. He cannot help it. It is the first thing the boy has said that sounds exactly like Qinghe.

"All right," he says. "Hello first."

* * *

The Gate wall opens like a pool.

It does not part, or crack, or glow. It simply becomes, between one breath and the next, a different kind of thing, a vast flat dark surface that is no longer stone but water, still and deep. He feels it in his teeth. Behind him, the family has taken one step back. Qinghe's hand is on her throat. The third stone in his lap has begun to burn, quietly, with a clear white light, like a coal.

"Now," says Pebble.

He lifts the paper. He does not read it. The boy does. They say it together, in one breath, two voices in one throat, the old one low and cracked and the young one high and clear, and the words go out of him and into the black surface like drops of ink, spreading, sinking, drawn down. Dear Mr. Cole. My name is Lin Jian. He feels them go. He feels the third stone burn down in his lap. He feels a vast silent attention turn, from somewhere on the far side of the dark, as a sleeper turns on a pillow.

Thank you for asking.

The last word leaves him. The surface closes over it. For a long moment nothing happens. The white light flickers and fades. The stone in his lap crumbles, quietly, into a heap of gray ash, and the Gate wall is a wall.

There is a sound, far down in the rock, like a very large door being closed by a very careful hand.

The panel goes gray. Then it goes blank. He watches the last line fade, and there is a moment of pure cold, a sense of a limb going numb. Then it passes. He draws a breath. He is sitting on a stone floor in a damp cellar in front of a plain black wall, and he is an old man with white hair and a Golden Core.

Still here, says the boy.

Still here.

That wasn't so bad.

He laughs, shakily. Qinghe is beside him already, with a cup of tea, and he takes it, and it is hot, and he drinks.

* * *

They wait for eleven hours.

Nobody leaves. It is not a decision; it is a kind of tide. The ring of watchers sits down, one by one, on the floor of the Dock. Zhao nurses the baby. Bell, who is thirty-seven and a doctor, unpacks her bandages and begins, with great firmness, to feed people. Qinghe produces a stove from somewhere, and a pot, and the Dock fills slowly with the smell of rice and ginger. Feng lies on his litter by the wall with his head tilted, listening. Tian Mo stands.

At dusk, Ning Ruiyan comes down the stair with a roll of paper and a lantern, and sits at the edge of the circle with his scarred face turned up to the ceiling as though he could see through it.

"The ring is open," he says softly. "It has been open for four nights. The sky has not closed. There is a thin line of light between the stars, very faint, very straight, and it is falling toward the Garden. It looks, Keeper..." He searches for the word. "It looks like a road."

Jian says nothing. Beside him, the boy sits at the table in the round room, with his hands folded, looking out of the window at the winter orchard. He has not spoken for an hour.

Are you afraid? Jian asks.

A bit.

What of?

That he won't answer. The dark eyes do not turn. Or that he will.

* * *

While they wait, the boy asks Qinghe for a story.

It is late. The ring of watchers has thinned to a few dozen, scattered on quilts around the stove, and the lamps have been turned down. Jian sits propped against the cot with Qinghe beside him. Wenyuan, on the litter by the wall, breathes slow and deep. Nobody is speaking much.

Can you ask her? says the boy, in the room, in the very small voice he uses when he wants something badly. The one about the stone. The one she used to tell.

He hesitates. Then he asks, aloud, "Mother. Do you remember the one about the boy and the stone?"

She goes still. "Which of you wants it?"

"Both, I think."

"Ah." Her hand finds his hair, and strokes it, in a slow absent rhythm. "Well. There was once a family on a hill. They were poor. They had a cart and a cow and an apple tree, and in the winter they were hungry. And one day the mother was digging under the tree for roots, and she turned up a stone. It was small and smooth and gray. And it was warm."

"How warm?"

"As warm as a hand. She took it home. She put it on the shelf. And in the night it began to hum." Her voice has dropped into the old cadence, soft and dry and sure. "The father said, throw it away. But the mother said, no. It is somebody's. Somebody will come for it. So they kept it. And one winter a baby was born in the house, a very small, very quiet one, who never cried."

"Why not?"

"He was listening." Her eyes close. "He had a great deal to hear. When he was a year old he picked the stone off the shelf and put it in his mouth, and it did not hurt him. And the mother said, oh. So you are the one it was for. And she put him to bed with the stone under his pillow. And the stone hummed him to sleep. And every night after that, he slept very soundly. Because he was never alone."

The Dock is quiet. Far down in the room behind his eyes, the boy is breathing slowly.

That's the one, he says, drowsily. That's the whole one.

Yes.

She always changed the end.

What was the end?

I don't know, says the boy. It was different every time. But the stone was always there.

* * *

It comes at the third watch.

He is half asleep, propped against the cot, with Qinghe's shoulder under his cheek and the rice pot long since empty. He wakes because the Dock has changed. The air has thickened, like air before a storm. The lamps in the niches have gone from blue to white. The Gate wall, black and smooth and ordinary, is giving off a faint cold light, the pale silver of the line in the sky, and on its surface, very slowly, characters are beginning to appear.

They are not written in plum ink. They are not in the Order's careful script. They rise out of the stone like breath on a window, in a quick untidy hand, sloping and blotched and hurried, the hand of a man who is writing at a desk in the dark with his heart in his mouth.

"Yue," he says.

She is already awake. She has her palm flat against the wall. Her gray eyes are wide. Pebble's voice, relaying, is gentle: I hear him. He is crying.

The family is on its feet. Nobody speaks. The writing grows down the wall, line after line, and in the silence a voice reads it, not aloud, but in the heads of everyone in the room: tired, kind, a little frightened, the voice of a man who has been rehearsing this for six hundred years and has forgotten all of it.

Dear Lin Jian.

Not Operator. Not Eight. Not "the copy." You. I've been calling you that for a very long time, and I never knew your name.

I'm going to try to say this properly. I've got one page, and I've been awake for about forty minutes, and I have a lot to cover.

First: thank you. I was not ready for it. Nobody ever wrote back. I built the thing so that someone could, and nobody ever did, and I stopped looking. Then somebody asked how the child was, in my sleep, and I woke up.

Second: I'm not sorry. I've been telling myself I am for six centuries, and it isn't true. I'm not sorry that you exist. I'm sorry for the cost. I'm sorry that you had to find out in a cellar, and I'm sorry about the names, and I'm sorry that nobody warned your mother.

Third, and I want you to hold this one. You asked in your letter, or you will, about the others.

Jian's heart stops. He does not breathe. In the room behind his eyes, the boy has risen from his chair.

I don't know what happened to the first seven. I swear. I thought they died. The Gate told me they died. The system flags a restore and sends the stored copy over the working one, and I thought the child went with it. I've never forgiven myself. But I've been awake for forty minutes now, and the first thing I did, the first thing, was look.

They didn't die.

They're here.

They're all here. Seven children. Seven Lin Jians, or whatever they were called, each in his own bed, in the Hall of the Sixth Door, in the first world, asleep. They've been asleep for six hundred years. The Gate carried them home when the Operators died, and kept them, and it never told me. They're not old. They're not hurt. They're waiting.

They're waiting for someone to come and wake them.

The writing slows. The hand shakes. He can see it, almost, the long blotched strokes, the places where the ink has run.

The sixth door is open now. Pebble opened it. He doesn't know I know. Tell him I'm sorry about the cold, and thank him for staying. You'll find the key in the last place I'd have looked. Come soon. I don't know how long the Gate will hold. It's eating itself.

Come as yourselves. Don't come as the copy. Don't come as the child. Come as both.

And Lin Jian.

I'd like to meet the tree.

Ethan Cole.

The last stroke fades. The wall is black. In the Dock, the lamps burn low. No one has made a sound.

Pebble has been silent through the whole of it. When the last line has faded, he slips from Yue's shoulder and walks slowly across the flags, on his four short gray legs, to the foot of the wall. He stands there with his cracked back to them and his small head raised. The white line down his spine pulses once, twice, like a heart.

"He said the sixth door is open," he says, in the deep voice. "I did not know that I had opened it."

"You told us, on the night of the Core," says Yue, signing.

"I said that it was open." The black eyes turn. "I did not know what I meant. I remembered the bronze, and the scarred hand, and the words. Stay until the gardener comes. I thought the gardener was a man. I thought he would arrive with a spade." The creature's voice wavers. "He was not a man. He was a family. He was a child, and a child, and a woman with a ladle, and an old man who falls asleep in winter. He was a thing that grows."

"Pebble," says Jian.

"I have waited six hundred years," says Pebble. "It was not so long. I had the cold, and the dark, and the thought of the hand. I would do it again." He turns, at last, and his face is small and gray and entirely without fear. "But I should like to see the door."

Then, in the dark, the boy speaks. His voice is very small and very clear, and it is not coming out of Jian's mouth, but out of the air, out of the stone, out of everywhere, and in the stunned silence, every person in that cellar hears it.

"Seven," he whispers. "There are seven of us."

Beside him, on the floor, a hundred and five years old, Qinghe has taken both his hands. Her face is wet. Her eyes are very bright.

"Then we had better go and fetch them," she says.
